quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on cost drivers, cost behaviour, inventories and the cost of goods sold.

questions.q: What is a cost driver?
options: Any cost that cannot be traced to a product
Any factor whose level, when changed, changes the total cost of a cost object
The person who approves spending in a department
The total cost divided by the number of units
questions.explain: A cost driver is any factor that affects total cost — units produced, machine set-ups or advertisements. Untraceable costs are indirect costs, and total cost ÷ units is the unit cost, not a driver.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a variable cost?
options: It changes per unit as output changes
It stays the same in total whatever the output
It changes in total in proportion to changes in a cost driver
It is any cost paid in cash
questions.explain: A variable cost changes in total in proportion to the driver; per unit it is roughly constant. The cost that stays the same in total is the fixed cost.

questions.q: Which of these is the best example of a fixed cost for a spinning mill?
options: Electricity that rises with spindle hours
questions.explain: Building depreciation does not change in total when output changes. Cotton, packing and power that rises with running hours all move with the cost driver and are variable.

questions.q: A unit cost is a single, unambiguous figure for any product.
questions.explain: The lecture warns that a unit cost is some total cost divided by some number of units — you must always ask which total and which units, because different choices give different unit costs.

questions.q: Goods that have been partly worked on but are not yet complete are called
questions.explain: Work in process is partly completed production. Finished goods are fully completed but unsold; merchandise is stock bought for resale without further work.

questions.q: Finished goods inventory consists of goods that are
options: Fully completed but not yet sold
questions.explain: Finished goods are completed products still in stock. Partly completed goods are work in process, and goods bought for resale are merchandise inventory.

questions.q: A merchandising business computes cost of goods sold as beginning inventory plus purchases minus ending inventory.
questions.explain: A merchandiser has no production, so the goods it sold are simply the opening stock plus what it bought, less what is still on the shelf at the end.

questions.q: In a manufacturer's cost of goods sold calculation, which item replaces the merchandiser's 'purchases'?
options: Manufacturing costs incurred during the period
questions.explain: A manufacturer adds cost of goods manufactured (goods completed and moved into finished goods) to beginning finished goods. Manufacturing costs incurred is an earlier subtotal before adjusting for work in process.

questions.q: Which of the following is an indirect manufacturing cost?
questions.explain: Plant equipment depreciation sits in the indirect manufacturing cost group with indirect labour, supplies, utilities and miscellaneous. Direct materials and direct labour are traced directly; COGM is a total, not a cost item.

questions.q: The number of machine set-ups can be a cost driver even though it is not a count of units produced.
questions.explain: The lecture lists units produced, machine set-ups and advertisements as examples of cost drivers; any factor that changes total cost qualifies, not only output volume.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How the schedule of cost of goods manufactured chains together, and how costs move when the driver moves.

questions.q: Direct materials used is calculated as
questions.explain: Materials available for use = beginning inventory + purchases; subtracting the ending inventory gives what was actually used. Reversing the signs on beginning and ending stock is a common error.

questions.q: Cost of goods manufactured equals
options: Manufacturing costs incurred + beginning WIP − ending WIP
Manufacturing costs incurred − beginning WIP + ending WIP
Cost of goods available for sale − ending finished goods
questions.explain: Costs incurred this period plus the opening work in process are the total to account for; the part still unfinished (ending WIP) is deducted. The last option is cost of goods sold, one stage further on.

questions.q: If output doubles, what happens to total variable cost and total fixed cost respectively?
questions.explain: Total variable cost moves in proportion to the driver, so it doubles; total fixed cost does not change in total with the driver.

questions.q: As output rises, the fixed cost per unit
questions.explain: The same total fixed cost is spread over more units, so each unit carries less. Students often confuse this with the variable cost per unit, which stays roughly constant.

questions.q: Manufacturing costs incurred during the period = direct materials used + direct manufacturing labour + indirect manufacturing cost.
questions.explain: These three groups make up the costs put into production during the period, before adjusting for opening and closing work in process.

questions.q: Cost of goods available for sale is
options: Beginning finished goods + cost of goods manufactured
Cost of goods manufactured − ending finished goods
questions.explain: The goods a manufacturer could have sold are the opening finished goods plus what was completed in the period. Subtracting ending finished goods then gives cost of goods sold.

questions.q: If ending work in process is larger than beginning work in process, cost of goods manufactured will be
options: Equal to cost of goods sold
questions.explain: COGM = costs incurred + beginning WIP − ending WIP, so a net increase in WIP means some of this period's cost is still on the floor and COGM is lower than costs incurred.

questions.q: Unit variable cost normally stays about the same when the cost driver changes, while total variable cost changes.
questions.explain: Proportional behaviour means total variable cost = unit variable cost × driver level; it is the total that moves, not the per-unit amount.

questions.q: A unit cost quoted as 'Rs 142 per metre' is meaningful only when you also know
options: Which total cost and which number of units were used
questions.explain: The lecture's warning: a unit cost is some total divided by some units. A unit cost that includes allocated fixed cost at one volume will differ from one at another volume or with a different cost total.

questions.q: Which quantity does NOT appear in the manufacturer's cost of goods sold formula?
questions.explain: Material purchases enter the schedule much earlier, in computing direct materials used. The COGS line uses only finished-goods stocks and cost of goods manufactured.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Work through the schedule of cost of goods manufactured and sold with the lecture's figures and a few new ones.

questions.q: Direct materials available for use were Rs 84,000 and direct materials used were Rs 76,000. What was the ending inventory of direct materials?
questions.explain: Materials used = available − ending inventory, so ending inventory = 84,000 − 76,000 = Rs 8,000.

questions.q: Manufacturing costs incurred during the period were Rs 105,000 and total manufacturing costs to account for were Rs 111,000. What was the beginning work in process?
questions.explain: Total to account for = costs incurred + beginning WIP, so beginning WIP = 111,000 − 105,000 = Rs 6,000.

questions.q: Total manufacturing costs to account for were Rs 111,000 and cost of goods manufactured was Rs 104,000. What was the ending work in process?
questions.explain: COGM = total to account for − ending WIP, so ending WIP = 111,000 − 104,000 = Rs 7,000.

questions.q: Cost of goods manufactured was Rs 104,000 and cost of goods available for sale was Rs 126,000. What was the beginning finished goods inventory?
questions.explain: Available for sale = beginning finished goods + COGM, so beginning finished goods = 126,000 − 104,000 = Rs 22,000.

questions.q: Cost of goods available for sale was Rs 126,000 and cost of goods sold was Rs 108,000. What was the ending finished goods inventory?
questions.explain: COGS = available for sale − ending finished goods, so ending finished goods = 126,000 − 108,000 = Rs 18,000.

questions.q: Direct materials used were Rs 76,000, direct manufacturing labour Rs 14,000 and indirect manufacturing cost Rs 15,000. What were the manufacturing costs incurred during the period?
questions.explain: Costs incurred = 76,000 + 14,000 + 15,000 = Rs 105,000, matching the lecture schedule.

questions.q: A merchandiser had beginning inventory Rs 40,000, purchases Rs 250,000 and ending inventory Rs 55,000. What was its cost of goods sold?
A mill's total cost of Rs 2,400,000 for a month covered 60,000 metres of fabric. What is the unit cost per metre?
questions.explain: Unit cost = total cost ÷ units = 2,400,000 ÷ 60,000 = Rs 40 per metre.

questions.q: Manufacturing costs incurred Rs 105,000; beginning WIP Rs 6,000; ending WIP Rs 7,000. Cost of goods manufactured is
questions.explain: COGM = 105,000 + 6,000 − 7,000 = Rs 104,000. Rs 106,000 comes from swapping the beginning and ending WIP; Rs 118,000 from adding both.

questions.q: A unit's fixed cost is Rs 300,000 a month and variable cost is Rs 25 per metre. At 20,000 metres the total cost per metre is
questions.explain: Total cost = 300,000 + 25 × 20,000 = 800,000; ÷ 20,000 = Rs 40 per metre (Rs 15 fixed + Rs 25 variable). Rs 25 ignores the fixed cost.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Costing-office situations where the ideas of this lecture decide what number you report and what it means.

questions.q: A weaving shed's accountant wants a driver for the cost of warp sizing chemicals. The most sensible choice is
questions.explain: A cost driver should be the factor whose level changes the cost; size consumption rises with the length of warp sized, not with headcount or customers.

questions.q: A mill ran at half its normal output last month and its reported cost per bag rose sharply. The most likely reason is
options: Fixed costs were spread over fewer bags
The accountant made an arithmetic error
questions.explain: Total fixed cost is unchanged, so halving output roughly doubles the fixed cost per bag. Variable cost per bag normally stays about the same.

questions.q: At the month end a dyeing plant has 20,000 m of fabric in the padding and steaming line. On the schedule this belongs to
questions.explain: Fabric still in the process is partly worked on, so its cost is ending WIP; it is deducted when computing cost of goods manufactured.

questions.q: A manager compares two mills using cost per bag and finds Mill A cheaper. Before accepting this, the costing office should first check
options: That both mills used the same definition of total cost and the same unit
questions.explain: A unit cost depends on which total and which units were chosen; if one mill includes depreciation and the other does not, or one counts bags of 100 lb and the other of 45.36 kg, the comparison is meaningless.

questions.q: A trading house that buys finished bedsheets and resells them should use the manufacturer's schedule with work-in-process lines.
questions.explain: A merchandiser has no production, so its cost of goods sold is simply beginning merchandise inventory + purchases − ending inventory; there is no WIP or cost of goods manufactured.

questions.q: A garment unit's stitching labour is paid per piece. For costing purposes this cost is
options: Fixed, because wages are always paid
Variable, because the total rises with pieces stitched
Indirect, because it cannot be traced
questions.explain: Piece-rate labour changes in total in proportion to output, so it is variable; it is also direct labour because it is traceable to the garments.

questions.q: Which of these would most increase a mill's cost of goods manufactured for the month, all else equal?
options: A larger ending work in process
A larger beginning work in process
A larger ending finished goods inventory
A larger beginning finished goods inventory
questions.explain: COGM = costs incurred + beginning WIP − ending WIP; more opening WIP means more cost completed this month. Finished-goods stocks affect cost of goods sold, not COGM.

questions.q: A costing office reports: beginning finished goods Rs 350,000, cost of goods manufactured Rs 2,150,000, ending finished goods Rs 410,000. Cost of goods sold for the month is?
The plant manager asks why building depreciation appears in the schedule when 'no cash was paid this month'. The right answer is
options: It is an indirect manufacturing cost of the period regardless of cash timing
It is part of cost of goods sold only when the building is sold
questions.explain: Depreciation of the plant building is listed among indirect manufacturing costs; it is a cost of using the asset this period even though the cash left years ago.

questions.q: A sales manager wants to advertise more. Under this lecture's definitions, the number of advertisements is
options: A cost driver for advertising cost
questions.explain: The lecture names advertisements as an example of a cost driver: changing their number changes the total cost of the related cost object.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step reasoning and common slips across the whole lecture — read each question carefully.

questions.q: Beginning direct materials inventory Rs 11,000, purchases Rs 73,000, ending materials Rs 8,000, direct labour Rs 14,000, indirect manufacturing cost Rs 15,000, beginning WIP Rs 6,000, ending WIP Rs 7,000. Cost of goods manufactured?
A student computes cost of goods manufactured as Rs 106,000 when costs incurred were Rs 105,000, beginning WIP Rs 6,000 and ending WIP Rs 7,000. Their mistake was
options: Adding ending WIP and subtracting beginning WIP
questions.explain: 105,000 − 6,000 + 7,000 = 106,000, so the signs were swapped. The correct figure is 105,000 + 6,000 − 7,000 = Rs 104,000.

questions.q: A mill's monthly fixed cost is Rs 900,000 and variable cost is Rs 30 per kg. Output falls from 60,000 kg to 45,000 kg. By how many rupees does the total cost per kg rise? Give the answer to two decimals.
questions.explain: At 60,000 kg: 15 + 30 = Rs 45; at 45,000 kg: 20 + 30 = Rs 50. The rise is Rs 5 per kg, all from fixed cost spread over fewer kg.

questions.q: If a manufacturer's ending finished goods inventory is higher than its beginning finished goods inventory, cost of goods sold is less than cost of goods manufactured.
questions.explain: COGS = beginning FG + COGM − ending FG; a net build-up of finished stock means part of this period's production was not sold, so COGS < COGM.

questions.q: Two unit costs for the same yarn — Rs 490 per bag last month and Rs 530 this month — with identical material and labour prices per bag. The most likely explanation is
options: Output this month was lower so fixed cost per bag rose
The ending finished goods were larger
questions.explain: With variable cost per bag unchanged, a higher unit cost points to fixed cost spread over fewer bags. Finished-goods stock levels do not change the cost per bag manufactured.

questions.q: Cost of goods available for sale was Rs 126,000, beginning finished goods Rs 22,000 and ending finished goods Rs 18,000. What was the cost of goods manufactured?
questions.explain: Available for sale = beginning FG + COGM, so COGM = 126,000 − 22,000 = Rs 104,000. The ending finished goods figure is not needed for this step.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly shows the flow of cost through a manufacturer?
options: Finished goods → work in process → materials → cost of goods sold
Materials → work in process → finished goods → cost of goods sold
Materials → finished goods → work in process → cost of goods sold
Work in process → materials → finished goods → cost of goods sold
questions.explain: The manufacturing statement flows from materials into work in process, then to finished goods when completed, and to cost of goods sold when sold.

questions.q: Beginning WIP Rs 6,000, ending WIP Rs 7,000, cost of goods manufactured Rs 104,000, direct materials used Rs 76,000, direct labour Rs 14,000. What was the indirect manufacturing cost?
questions.explain: Costs incurred = COGM + ending WIP − beginning WIP = 104,000 + 7,000 − 6,000 = 105,000; indirect cost = 105,000 − 76,000 − 14,000 = Rs 15,000.

questions.q: A cost that is Rs 50,000 a month at 10,000 m, Rs 50,000 at 15,000 m and Rs 50,000 at 20,000 m is
questions.explain: The total does not change as the driver (metres) changes, which is the definition of a fixed cost. A variable cost would rise from 10,000 m to 20,000 m.

questions.q: The sales department wants cost of goods sold for a month in which 2,000 bags were manufactured, 300 bags were in opening finished stock and 500 bags in closing finished stock. How many bags' cost goes into cost of goods sold?
questions.explain: Bags sold = 300 + 2,000 − 500 = 1,800, mirroring beginning FG + COGM − ending FG. 2,200 comes from swapping the opening and closing stock.
